assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turned precision spectroscopy into a new regime of measurement: magic-wavelength trapping removes motional and light-shift errors while many atoms interrogated in parallel give very high stability. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 open redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and fundamental-constant tests. Conceptually original and clearly bounded; this is what we can measure and how accurately, squarely in laser spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice concept and demonstrated early Sr lattice clocks; Ye's group drove accuracy and stability records and the comb-linked clock programme. The two-name credit is clean and supports a fair prize, though the wider optical-clock field (ion clocks, comb precedent, other lattice groups) means some credit lies outside the pair.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups reproduce lattice clocks at the 1e-18 level and international clock comparisons are routine; the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Boundary with the 2005 comb prize and with optical ion clocks is a matter of framing.
The redefinition of the second has not yet taken place.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent interfaces between light and matter (cavity QED single-atom photon control, EIT and slow-light storage, quantum memories, elementary network links) underpin quantum repeaters and networks. The physics is deep and original, and I know from my own work on optical quantum memories how much depends on this line. The field is broad, so a prize needs a crisp core.
assessment.attribution: Kimble led early cavity QED and the quantum-network vision; Rempe's single-atom cavity photon sources and network nodes; Lukin's EIT-based storage. Credit is plausible but compound, and storage pioneers outside the list (Hau, Harris and ensemble or rare-earth memory groups) also contributed. The trio is defensible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Individual elements are well confirmed (photon storage, atom-photon entanglement, node-to-node links). Full quantum networks remain proof-of-principle, so the combined concept is not fully mature.
uncertainties: Compound field whose parts may need different recognition.
Credit for light storage is shared with people not listed.
Lukin appears under several candidates and the credit mix is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realising the Hubbard model with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (superfluid to Mott transition, single-site imaging, fermionic Hubbard physics) created a controllable quantum simulator for many-body physics. Originality, clarity and impact across AMO and condensed matter are high. How far results go beyond classical computation remains open.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and Cirac) proposed the realisation; Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition; Esslinger realised fermionic physics. Five names for at most three slots, so allocation is a real problem; this configuration pairs theory with experiment but leaves out Greiner and Cirac. Jaksch is not on the list and I cannot resolve that from the supplied text.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are widely reproduced and the platform is mature. Quantum-simulation advantage and new physics are still developing, so recognition is on time but the strongest payoff may lie ahead.
uncertainties: Five credited names for at most three laureates; attribution unresolved.
Overlap with candidate B023 (Cirac and Zoller) and with Rydberg-array simulators.
Extent of quantum advantage for Hubbard physics is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry gives inertial, gravitational and constants measurements with matter-wave phase sensitivity (gravimetry, gradiometry, h/m for the fine-structure constant, equivalence-principle tests). A clear, original use of laser cooling and coherent manipulation, well within atomic physics and precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of light-pulse interferometers, Pritchard's early atom-optics demonstrations and Kasevich's gravimetry and gradiometry form the core. Steven Chu is not on the list, so the supplied credit is imperfect; the chosen three are the best fit among supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in laboratories and in field gravimeters. Large-baseline fundamental-physics tests are still developing, so applications are young but the core method is mature.
uncertainties: Absence of Steven Chu from the credited names complicates fair attribution.
Overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling prize.
Fundamental-physics reach (dark matter, gravitational waves) not yet demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED gave strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave resonators and enabled dispersive readout, gates and the leading superconducting quantum-computing architecture. Importance and impact are high; the idea of transplanting cavity QED to circuits is clear and original.
assessment.attribution: Blais with Girvin and others made the theory; Wallraff and Schoelkopf with the Yale group demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. Girvin is not credited here and Devoret also mattered. The supplied trio is reasonable, but recent recognition of macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits touches adjacent ground.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups and used in industrial devices. Technology is moving quickly, so recognition is timely, though some would wait for fault-tolerance milestones.
uncertainties: Adjacent to a recent prize for superconducting circuit quantum effects.
Missing names (Girvin, Devoret) complicate the configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade in optically trapped atom arrays with programmable tweezers has delivered large quantum simulators and high-fidelity gates. A strong, original AMO development linked to my interest in light-matter control.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Lukin proposed blockade gates; Browaeys and Lukin and others demonstrated arrays and many-body physics. Other groups (Weiss, Endres, Bernien) and theorists (Jaksch) also matter, and allocation is delicate because the field is moving fast.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across several groups, but the field is young and error-corrected computation is not established; recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: The key contributors may be redefined within a few years.
Overlap of Lukin with candidates B042 and B043.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and coherent control of single diamond defect spins supports room-temperature quantum sensing and entangled links between distant nodes. Importance is high, bridging quantum optics, solid state and metrology.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's single-NV optical detection, Awschalom's coherent control and spin photonics, and Hanson's entanglement and loophole-free Bell test. Walsworth and Lukin made major sensing contributions that cannot fit in three slots, so credit is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced with widespread applications in sensing, though some network and biomedical claims are still developing.
uncertainties: Five credited names for three slots.
Partial overlap with the 2022 Bell-test prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol) is foundational at the intersection of quantum optics, information theory and cryptography, with implementations in fibre and satellite links. Originality and lasting influence are clear.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84 and Ekert the entanglement-based protocol, a natural three-person split. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a possible further credit outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Demonstrated by many groups, though side-channel security and large-scale deployment are still evolving. The 2022 prize recognised entanglement tests, which partly overlaps.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize.
Wiesner's precedence and its effect on attribution is unresolved.
Physics versus computer-science boundary.
